claim: Random search with a fixed budget of k evaluations will, in expectation, find an architecture in the top 100/k% of the search space, establishing the theoretically correct estimand as expected-best-of-k rather than mean-of-population.
stance_target: correct statistical estimand for NAS search-method evaluation (Q3)
scope_conditions: general NAS random-search baseline theory, applies to any tabular/queryable search space
quoted_support: "random search with a budget of k evaluations will, in expectation, find architectures in the top 100/k% of the search space."
time_period: 2023 survey, citing Sciuto et al. 2020, Li and Talwalkar 2019, Yang et al. 2020, Chen et al. 2018

claim: Random search performance as a NAS baseline is search-space-dependent: it is surprisingly strong on highly engineered search spaces with a high fraction of strong architectures but performs poorly on large, diverse search spaces.
stance_target: bounds how strong a 'beats random search' claim is without characterizing the search space
scope_conditions: citing Sciuto et al. 2020, Li and Talwalkar 2019, Yang et al. 2020, Chen et al. 2018 (strong case) vs. Bender et al. 2020, Real et al. 2020 (weak case)
quoted_support: "multiple papers have shown that random search performs surprisingly well... However, other works show that random search does not perform well on large, diverse search spaces (Bender et al. 2020; Real et al. 2020)."

claim: NAS best-practices literature (Li and Talwalkar 2019; Yang et al. 2020; Lindauer and Hutter 2020) mandates a specific checklist for sound, reproducible, statistically fair NAS comparisons, formalized as a checklist researchers are urged to attach to paper appendices.
stance_target: methodology standards a 2025-2026 NAS reviewer would demand of the target paper (Q3)
scope_conditions: NAS research broadly, checklist from Lindauer and Hutter 2020 (JMLR)
quoted_support: "Recently, a few papers have laid out best practices and guidelines for conducting sound NAS research that is reproducible and makes fair comparisons (Li and Talwalkar 2019; Yang et al. 2020; Lindauer and Hutter 2020). These best practices are also available as a checklist (Lindauer and Hutter 2020). We encourage NAS researchers to follow the checklist and to attach it to the appendix of their papers."

claim: NAS best practices require releasing full code including random seeds, releasing both search-stage and final-evaluation training pipelines (which often differ), and reporting whether/how the NAS method's own hyperparameters were tuned.
stance_target: specific reproducibility requirements the target paper must satisfy or fail
quoted_support: "It is nearly impossible to reproduce NAS methods without the full code. Even then, random seeds should be specified and reported... Many papers use different architecture training pipelines during the search and during the final evaluation, so it is important to include both."

claim: When comparing NAS methods, using 'the same datasets' is insufficient; researchers must use the exact same fixed benchmark (train-test split, search space, evaluation pipeline), always compare against random sampling and random search baselines, run thorough ablations isolating which components drive improvement, and run multiple trials reporting seeds because NAS algorithms can have high variance requiring statistical-significance verification.
stance_target: direct checklist against which the target paper's methodology (single search space, unspecified seed count, sequential single-context generation) should be tested (Q3)
quoted_support: "When comparing NAS methods, it is not enough to use the same datasets. The exact same NAS benchmarks must be used... it is important to compare the method with baselines such as random sampling and random search... we recommend that researchers run multiple trials of their experiments and report the random seeds for each experiment. NAS methods can have high variance in the randomness of the algorithm, so running many trials is important to verify statistically significant comparisons."

claim: Over-reliance on a small number of NAS benchmarks causes field-level overfitting and is not conducive to discovering genuinely novel methods; researchers should use a large, diverse set of NAS benchmarks whenever possible.
stance_target: critique the target paper faces if it evaluates on only a single CNN search space/benchmark
scope_conditions: citing Raji et al. 2021, Koch et al. 2021
quoted_support: "over-reliance on a few benchmarks can lead to the field over-fitting (Raji et al. 2021; Koch et al. 2021) and is not conducive to the discovery of truly novel methods. Therefore, researchers should use a large set of diverse NAS benchmarks whenever possible."

claim: The canonical tabular NAS benchmark landscape as of 2023 comprises NAS-Bench-101 (423,624 architectures, 3 seeds, CIFAR-10), NAS-Bench-201 (6,466 unique architectures across CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100/ImageNet-16-120, 3 seeds each), NATS-Bench (extends NAS-Bench-201 with a macro/size search space), Surr-NAS-Bench-DARTS/NAS-Bench-301 (surrogate benchmark from 60,000 trained architectures), NAS-Bench-Suite (unifies 28 benchmark tasks), and NAS-Bench-Suite-Zero (precomputed zero-cost proxies across all tasks).
stance_target: establishes exact benchmark identity/scale the query asks about (Q3)
scope_conditions: Section 8, citing Ying et al. 2019, Dong and Yang 2020, Dong et al. 2021b, Siems et al. 2020, Mehta et al. 2022, Krishnakumar et al. 2022
quoted_support: "The first tabular NAS benchmark was NAS-Bench-101... 423,624 architectures, each with precomputed validation and test accuracies on CIFAR-10 for three different seeds... NAS-Bench-201... consisting of 6466 unique architectures, each with precomputed validation and test accuracies on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-16-120 for three seeds each."

claim: The survey names the exact bibliographic identities of the three canonical NAS-evaluation-critique papers: Li and Talwalkar (2019) 'Random search and reproducibility for neural architecture search' (UAI), Yang, Esperança, Carlucci (2020) 'NAS evaluation is frustratingly hard' (ICLR), and Lindauer and Hutter (2020) 'Best practices for scientific research on neural architecture search' (JMLR), plus Sciuto et al. (2020) 'Evaluating the search phase of neural architecture search' (ICLR).
stance_target: establishes canonical citation targets for Q3 methodological-critique literature
quoted_support: "Li and Talwalkar (2019) Liam Li and Ameet Talwalkar. Random search and reproducibility for neural architecture search. In Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2019." / "Yang et al. (2020) Antoine Yang, Pedro M Esperança, and Fabio M Carlucci. Nas evaluation is frustratingly hard. In Proceedings of the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2020." / "Lindauer and Hutter (2020) Marius Lindauer and Frank Hutter. Best practices for scientific research on neural architecture search. In JMLR, 2020."
